**Finding submitted: deviation (IP — Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data).**

**What I found**
- **Article III (p0048)** gives Licensor all right, title and interest in the Licensed Technology and all Intellectual Property Rights therein. Combined with the very broad definitions of "Intellectual Property Rights" (p0008) and "Derivative Work" (p0005 — "additions, modifications, improvements or enhancements"), the **paid-for customisation work under Article VII(b) (p0087)** — a "unique client front end and other enhancements" we specify and pay for — lands entirely on Licensor's side with no licence back.
- Our only right is the **non-exclusive, Field-of-Use, term-limited licence** (p0030), which we may not modify (p0047) or sublicense (p0042), and which **terminates outright** with a return-of-materials obligation (p0138).
- **No Customer Data provision at all**: nothing confirms we retain our trade, order and market data. (The Confidential Information definition at p0004 runs one way only, protecting Licensor's information.)

**Why it fails the fallback**: the fallback requires a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense deliverables. We have the opposite — a revocable, non-transferable licence that dies with the Agreement.

**Redline (validated, ok:true)**: a single paragraph inserted after Article III that (i) confirms Licensee owns its data and pre-existing IP and that nothing assigns them to Licensor, and (ii) grants a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense Custom Deliverables, surviving termination.

I deliberately took the **fallback rather than preferred** position: because the customisations are enhancements bolted onto Licensor's own multi-licensee platform, demanding assignment of ownership would be disproportionate, and Licensor's ownership of the underlying platform is expressly fine under the playbook.
